segments: There is a thing you have watched
happen with your own eyes, in
somebody's kitchen, about twenty
minutes after the cake.
A boy you know is sitting on the floor
with a paper plate.
He is seven, he has been calm all
afternoon, and you would have said so
yourself.
Then the cake goes round, the icing is
blue, and there are cans of something
orange nobody is counting.
Fifteen minutes later a chair goes over,
and he is on the back of the sofa
shouting a word that is not a word.
His mother says the thing that you and
every adult in that room are already thinking.
Sugar.
Nobody taught you that.
You watched it happen, and you have
watched it in more than one kitchen,
which is what any of us mean when we
say we know a thing.
But your kitchen is not a study, and a
lot of people went and ran the study.
The design is simple enough to hold in
your head.
Give one child sugar,
give the next a sweetener close enough
that nobody can taste the difference,
and make sure nobody knows who got what.
Not the parents, not the teachers,
and not you.
They ran that design over and over.
three researchers gathered every trial
they could find:
sixteen write-ups, twenty-three trials
inside them, and that is twenty-three
chances for your kitchen to turn up in
the data. They found nothing:
no effect on how the children behaved,
and none on how they thought or paid
attention.
One trial took twenty-three children
whose parents had signed them up as
the sensitive ones,
fed them sugar for three weeks, and
scored them thirty-nine ways.
Not one of the thirty-nine moved, and
those parents were as sure as you are.
That result has held for thirty years.
The people who ran it were careful to
say a small effect could still be
hiding in there,
but the big one you saw in your
kitchen is not, and there is no honest
way around that.
So the correction goes out, and
underneath the politeness it tells you
that you made it up.
That is where the story stops, every time:
sugar and wild children is a myth.
And that ending is true, and it is
useless, because nobody has ever
believed it about themselves.
You do not walk out of that kitchen
and decide your own eyes are broken.
You are being told that millions of
people watched the same fifteen
minutes for fifty years and imagined
every one of them.
It is a shrug in a lab coat, and we
have all been on the wrong end of one.
So hold on to your kitchen.
Whatever went wrong here, your kitchen
is not the mistake,
and I am going to stay on your side of it.
So if your eyes are working, the
mistake has to sit somewhere in the
studies themselves.
Every one of those trials tested the child,
and not one of them tested the person
watching the child.
two researchers, Hoover and Milich,
did exactly that instead.
Thirty-five boys, five to seven years
old, about the age you are picturing,
each of them in with his mother.
You want to keep your eye on the mothers.
Every boy got the same drink, and
there was no sugar in the building.
They told half the mothers their son
had just had a large dose of sugar,
and the other half that he had been
given a placebo.
Same room, same drink, two sentences.
Afterwards, the mothers who heard the
sugar sentence rated their sons as
more wild, and the gap was big enough
to count.
On the tape, those mothers sat closer
to their sons and stayed there.
They leaned toward more talking and
more telling him off,
though that was a lean and not a
finding, and I will not sell it to you
as one.
But I have to stop and say
what that study is, because it is the
weakest thing I have shown you and it
carries the most.
Every mother in that room already
believed sugar
set her son off, and that
is how they got picked.
So: thirty-five boys,
one lab, mothers only,
no fathers, and every mother sure
before she walked in. And what it is good at
is the mother:
it tells you what she saw and what she did,
and it was never built to settle what
her son did back.
So you should hold the two halves differently:
twenty-three trials and thirty years
on one side,
one study on the other.
I want to keep going with it anyway,
and here is my reason.
In all the work on what sugar does to a child,
almost nobody pointed the camera at
the adult, and this one did. So
put my reason aside and look at the
tape again, because what those mothers
did is a loop.
Follow it round, and keep your eye on
her instead of the boy.
She hears the word sugar,
so she moves in closer than she would
have, and watches him harder,
and gets on at him sooner.
And a boy with an adult standing over him
gets wound up.
That last step is mine
and not the study's, and you should
know the difference.
But you have been five years old, and
so have I,
and you know exactly how that feels.
So she sees a wild boy, and she is not
lying, any more than you were.
She was never wrong about the room.
She was wrong about which person in it
had changed.
The belief did not describe the room,
it built the room, and everybody in it
watched it come true.
So this was never a mistake about sugar.
It was a mistake about seeing, and
that is a mistake you can make in any
room you walk into.
Here is the one thing you can never
see in a room,
and it is your own expectation of it.
Everything else in there comes with a
label on it.
Your expectation is the only thing you
brought in with you,
and it arrives dressed as the room.
You do not think, I have been told
this child is wild.
You think, look at that, the child is wild.
Which means you do not need a lab to
run that experiment,
because we run it on each other all week.
We have all handed somebody a sentence
about who they were about to be.
He is the shy one, she is difficult,
that one is a handful.
Then we stand a little closer, we
watch a little harder,
and we get exactly what we said we would.
We are not lying and we are not stupid.
We are simply the last people in the
room who could ever tell.
So go back to your kitchen, to the
blue icing, the paper plate, and the
boy on the back of the sofa.
Every single thing you saw was real.
The only thing we got wrong was where
in the room to look.
